1.title: Know the cleaning trade
1.intro: Cleaning services work for homes, offices, shops and shared buildings. Learn the types and the main words.
pts: Name types: home, office, post-construction, move-out, window, floor care.
Describe the difference between routine and deep cleaning.
Explain what germs, dirt and soil are and why each needs a different method.
List words: scope of work, quote, supplies, contact time, dwell time.
Classify a space by use and traffic, such as a quiet office or a busy shop, and say how this changes the visit.
Compare daily, weekly, monthly and quarterly tasks for one room.
Identify what the client values most: look, smell, health or cost.
1.ex: A small office wants a weekly clean. Scope: empty bins, clean kitchen and bathroom, vacuum, wipe desks; a deep clean is added once a quarter. Over 52 weeks, 4 deep cleans leave 48 routine-only visits, so the quote shows both kinds.
1.act: Walk through a small shop or office and list all areas that need cleaning and how often.
1.std: Task: list cleaning scope. Condition: one real space. Standard: all areas and frequencies listed on one page.

2.title: Chemicals, tools and safe method
2.intro: Cleaning uses chemicals that can harm. Read the label every time.
pts: Read the label and safety data sheet: hazard, dilution, contact time, first aid.
Apply the rule: never mix products and never move them into unlabelled bottles.
Choose gloves, eye cover and air flow for the task.
Compare cleaning, sanitising and disinfecting and use the right level.
Calculate a dilution from the label, such as 1 part product to 10 parts water.
Check that every spray bottle carries a label with the product name and hazard.
Carry products in a tray or bucket, and keep a spill kit ready.
2.ex: A disinfectant must stay wet on a surface for the time on the label to work. If the label says 1 part product to 10 parts water and 5 minutes contact time, a 550 mL bottle holds 50 mL of product and 500 mL of water. The cleaner sets a timer and wipes a test patch first.
2.act: Make a one-page product table: name, use, hazard, dilution, protection.
2.std: Task: choose products safely. Condition: three real products. Standard: all label data copied correctly and protection chosen.

3.title: Follow the rules in Canada
3.intro: Workplace, product and building rules apply. Check with the local authority.
pts: Explain that hazardous product labels and safety data sheets follow national standards.
Describe workplace health and safety training and reporting duties; check your province.
Check rules for waste and wastewater: do not pour chemicals into storm drains.
Apply business rules: city licence where needed, insurance, and tax records; check with local and federal bodies.
Identify the provincial workplace safety body and its rules on working alone.
Check whether your business needs workplace injury cover when you hire helpers; check the provincial rule.
Describe the duty to report an injury or chemical spill, and keep a written record.
3.ex: Rules table row: Waste disposal | city | use approved drop-off for chemicals | every time | receipt or note in file. A second row: Injury report | provincial workplace safety body | report and record within the time the body sets | every case | copy kept. Check the time limit on the official page and write the date checked.
3.act: Make a rules table for your city and province with official pages and dates.
3.std: Task: map the rules. Condition: official pages only. Standard: each row has an enforcer, an action and a checked date.

4.title: Clean to a measured standard
4.intro: Clients judge by results. Set a standard you can check.
pts: Build a checklist by area with pass or fail marks.
Check results by sight, touch and, where needed, a simple test.
Apply the same method each time and record time per area.
Fix a failed item on the spot and note why it failed.
Calculate the pass rate: items passed divided by items checked.
Photograph each area before and after on the first visit as a baseline.
Ask the client to sign off the checklist at the end of the first month.
4.ex: Office kitchen checklist: counters clear, sink clean, fridge wiped, floor dry, bin empty. On the first visit 4 of 5 pass, an 80% pass rate; the floor edges fail. The method changes to edges first, and the next visit passes 5 of 5, or 100%.
4.act: Clean one space twice, scoring with your checklist each time.
4.std: Task: clean to standard. Condition: written checklist. Standard: all items pass on the second run.

5.title: Floors, windows, bathrooms and kitchens
5.intro: Each area has its own method and risk.
pts: Apply floor care by type: vinyl, tile, wood, carpet; use the right product.
Use a safe window method; never lean out; use proper ladders or poles.
Clean bathrooms from clean to dirty areas, with separate cloths.
Place wet floor signs and dry the area.
Compare microfibre cloths, mops and squeegees for different floors and glass.
Check for slip risks such as wet tile, floor wax and wet entry mats.
Handle sharps and broken glass with tongs and a puncture-proof container, never bare hands.
5.ex: Mopping a hall: sign out first, mop back toward the exit, sign stays until dry. A hall 20 m long and 2 m wide is 40 square metres; at 10 square metres a minute that is 4 minutes of mopping plus drying time. No one slips and the client sees care.
5.act: Practice each area once and record the method, the product and the time.
5.std: Task: clean four area types. Condition: practice spaces. Standard: method, product and time recorded and no safety step skipped.

6.title: Quote, price and plan
6.intro: A good quote is clear on scope, price and time. A weak quote leads to loss.
pts: Measure the space and agree the scope in writing.
Compute cost per visit: time, supplies, travel, insurance, tax set-aside.
Compare per-hour and per-job quotes.
Plan routes and shifts with buffers for slow days.
Walk the space with the client and note extras such as inside windows or fridges.
Compute price per hour and per square metre and compare to test that the price is fair.
State exclusions in the quote, such as mould or biohazard removal.
6.ex: Price 95 per visit, supplies and travel 15. Margin = 95 - 15 = 80. If fixed costs are 700 a month, break-even is 700 / 80 = 8.75, so 9 visits (teaching numbers only).
6.act: Write two quotes for practice spaces and test the price with five people.
6.std: Task: quote a job. Condition: practice space. Standard: scope, price, frequency and exclusions on one page and margin shown.

7.title: Clients, contracts and quality
7.intro: Repeat clients are the strength of cleaning businesses. Reliability and records win them.
pts: Build a service agreement: scope, schedule, access, cancellation, damage.
Apply a quality check by visit, with photos and a score.
Handle complaints: listen, return to fix, record cause.
Track funnel: contacts, quotes, signed clients, repeats.
Create a short onboarding sheet for a new client: access, alarm, supplies and contact.
Calculate the signing rate: signed clients divided by quotes.
Ask for a referral after a good month.
7.ex: Four weeks: 25 contacts, 8 quotes, 3 signed. Contact to quote is 8 / 25 = 32%, and quote to signed is 3 / 8 = 37.5%. The weakest step is contact to quote; a short site visit may improve it.
7.act: Contact 20 local firms, book 5 quote visits and write an agreement.
7.std: Task: win and keep clients. Condition: four weeks. Standard: funnel recorded and signed agreement with scope and access.

8.title: Run the business for real
8.intro: Now run the cleaning service with real clients, a team plan and a growth plan.
pts: Run a 60-day pilot with a stop rule agreed in advance.
Review weekly: visits, margin, quality score, complaints, cash.
Create a 12-month plan with insurance, equipment and hiring steps.
Lead a team: train, check and coach using your standards.
Calculate cash left each week: money in minus costs.
Compare time per visit with the plan to find slow spots.
Write a safety and quality check for every new team member.
8.ex: Stop rule: if margin per visit is under 60 after 60 days, change the price or scope. With a price of 95 and actual costs of 17, the margin is 78, above 60, so the pilot continues. Adding one client in the same building saves travel.
8.act: Run the pilot, write the review and present your plan to three people.
8.std: Task: run a cleaning pilot. Condition: 60 days, real clients. Standard: results compared with the stop rule and safety training confirmed.

quiz: What is contact time?
The time a disinfectant must stay wet to work.
Where do you find chemical hazards?
The label and the safety data sheet.
What must you never do with cleaning products?
Mix them or move them to unlabelled bottles.
Why use a checklist with pass or fail?
To measure and repeat quality.
Which way do you clean a bathroom?
From clean to dirty areas with separate cloths.
Why use a wet floor sign?
To prevent slips until the floor is dry.
What belongs in a quote?
Scope, price, frequency and exclusions.
How do you find break-even visits?
Fixed cost divided by margin per visit.
Where should chemical waste go?
An approved drop-off, not a storm drain.
Who sets workplace safety rules?
Mostly the province; check your provincial body.
